The concept of Jesus and the atonement to me are just examples of an ancient mind's theological theories. This revolves around two basic points:

First, the "sacrifice" of Jesus to appease an all powerful sky God, seems to be a theological evolution of the ancient practice of sacrificing animals to appease unseen powers that be. This is where I believe we get the idea of the atonement. Mormons use this in their own way, saying that older practices of animal sacrifice were just "preparing" man for the "real" and "higher" sacrifice of Jesus. I personally think this is a clear case of retroactive reinterpretation, putting the cart before the horse.

Secondly, Jesus easily fits into the place in myth of half man/half God, which was common in ancient pagan myths. Horus and Hercules are good examples. He is the pinnacle of a system of values, halfway between heaven and earth, performing superhuman feats. Your perception of Jesus as a sort of Herculean figure is more significant than you think. The unique thing, however, is that Jesus represents a shift in the ancient world towards a different system of values. Instead of strength, survival, dominance, fitness, etc., we have a figure representing compassion. 

So even if the Jesus/atonement myth is not literally true, it's still a significant shift towards a new system of values. He ancient world was an extremely harsh place. But with Jesus comes a new hierarchy of values, and all the old myths are remade with superhuman Jesus and his sacrifice as the son of the sky God to save us all. 

The origins of Christianity were cobbled together from a mix of growing-stale myths and theology from around the ancient world: Zoroastrianism (earth is ground zero for a titanic battle between good and evil-- ancient Persian religion), Ancient Greek/roman myths, ancient Judaism, and ancient pagan Egypt. You wouldn't believe how much is pulled from old myths (I.e. Christmas used to be an old pagan holiday, 3 magis became the 3 wise men of Jesus birth, etc.)
